q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern of decolonization described in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the wave of independence after 1945.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between British and French decolonization.

sample_answers.a: One pattern was variety: some colonies won independence through negotiation, as in India and Ghana, while others required war, as in Algeria and Indochina — the method depended on the colonizer and local conditions.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the Second World War, which bankrupted European treasuries, mobilized millions of colonial soldiers who returned with new expectations, and made the cost of holding empires exceed the benefits.
sample_answers.c: Britain generally negotiated timetables for withdrawal and tried to preserve Commonwealth ties, while France fought to keep Algeria and Indochina as integral parts of France, leaving far bloodier legacies.

q1.stimulus: Decolonization took many forms: Britain negotiated withdrawals in India and Ghana, France fought losing wars in Indochina and Algeria, and Portugal clung to Angola until 1975. What the new nations shared was less a method than a moment — the Second World War had bankrupted the empires, armed and trained colonial soldiers, and exposed the gap between Allied promises of freedom and colonial reality. Nationalist leaders from Nehru to Nkrumah turned that gap into independence.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Jawaharlal Nehru, address on Indian independence, August 14, 1947
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE goal Nehru sets for independent India in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage reflects the challenges facing new nations in 1947.
parts.c: Explain ONE difference between India's independence and Ghana's independence a decade later.

sample_answers.a: Nehru pledges the new nation to ending poverty, ignorance, and inequality — framing independence as the start of a struggle for social justice, not just a flag-raising.
sample_answers.b: The passage reflects the enormity of the task: a partitioned subcontinent amid communal violence, with hundreds of millions in poverty — freedom meant inheriting catastrophe as well as sovereignty.
sample_answers.c: India won independence through decades of mass nationalist mobilization under the Congress, while Ghana's path was shorter and led by Nkrumah's Convention People's Party using strikes and boycotts — and Ghana became the model for sub-Saharan Africa, whereas India was the first great break.

q2.stimulus: [Paraphrase of Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny':] At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom. We pledge ourselves to the service of our millions — to ending poverty, ignorance, disease, and inequality of opportunity. This is not a moment of triumph alone, but a beginning.

q3.attribution: Photograph of Kwame Nkrumah addressing supporters, Gold Coast, 1950s
q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE detail of the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE way Nkrumah's movement illustrates the methods of decolonization in Africa.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity between the colonial period and the early independence period in Ghana.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows Nkrumah as a charismatic mass leader before a crowd — independence as a popular movement, not a backroom deal.
sample_answers.b: Nkrumah's Convention People's Party used 'positive action' — strikes, boycotts, and mass rallies — to make the Gold Coast ungovernable, forcing Britain to negotiate a timetable for independence.
sample_answers.c: One continuity was economic: independent Ghana still depended on exporting cocoa within trade structures built for colonial extraction, so political independence did not end economic dependence on world commodity markets.

q3.stimulus: Photograph of Kwame Nkrumah, leader of Ghana's independence movement, addressing supporters — Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, in 1957.
